questions.question: What is the main advantage of DBSCAN over K-Means clustering?
options: DBSCAN is always faster than K-Means
DBSCAN can find arbitrarily shaped clusters and doesn't require specifying the number of clusters
DBSCAN always produces better silhouette scores
DBSCAN works better with high-dimensional data
questions.explanation: DBSCAN's main advantages are its ability to discover clusters of arbitrary shapes (not just spherical) and automatically determine the number of clusters based on data density, unlike K-Means which requires you to specify K beforehand.

questions.question: In DBSCAN, what is a 'core point'?
options: The center of a cluster
A point that has at least MinPts points within distance ε
A point that is exactly ε distance from the cluster center
The first point selected in each cluster
questions.explanation: A core point is defined as a point that has at least MinPts points (including itself) within distance ε. Core points form the dense regions that define clusters in DBSCAN.

questions.question: What happens to points that are neither core points nor border points in DBSCAN?
options: They are assigned to the nearest cluster
They are classified as noise points
They form their own single-point clusters
They are removed from the dataset
questions.explanation: Points that are neither core points nor border points are classified as noise points (outliers). This is one of DBSCAN's key features - automatic outlier detection.

questions.question: If you increase the epsilon (ε) parameter in DBSCAN, what is the most likely effect?
options: More clusters will be formed
Fewer clusters will be formed
The algorithm will run faster
More points will be classified as noise
questions.explanation: Increasing ε makes the neighborhood radius larger, which means more points will be considered neighbors. This typically results in fewer, larger clusters as previously separate clusters may merge together.

questions.question: What is a 'border point' in DBSCAN?
options: A point at the edge of the dataset
A point that defines cluster boundaries
A non-core point that is within ε distance of a core point
A point that belongs to multiple clusters
questions.explanation: A border point is a non-core point (has fewer than MinPts neighbors) that is within distance ε of at least one core point. Border points belong to clusters but are on the periphery.

questions.question: Which parameter in DBSCAN controls the minimum density required to form a cluster?
options: Epsilon (ε)
MinPts
Both ε and MinPts together
The distance metric
questions.explanation: Both ε and MinPts together control the minimum density. ε defines the neighborhood size, and MinPts defines how many points must be in that neighborhood to be considered dense enough to form a cluster.

questions.question: In which scenario would DBSCAN likely perform better than K-Means?
options: When you know exactly how many clusters you want
When clusters are perfectly spherical and well-separated
When you have crescent-shaped or elongated clusters with outliers
When you need the fastest possible clustering algorithm
questions.explanation: DBSCAN excels with non-spherical cluster shapes (like crescents or elongated clusters) and automatically handles outliers by marking them as noise, while K-Means assumes spherical clusters and is sensitive to outliers.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of DBSCAN in the worst case?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n³)
questions.explanation: DBSCAN has O(n²) time complexity in the worst case because it needs to compute distances between all pairs of points to find neighborhoods. However, with spatial indexing structures like KD-trees, this can be improved to O(n log n).
